The royal tern nests on island beaches or isolated beaches with limited predators.
The western population nests from California to Mexico and winters from California south to Peru.
The royal tern has few predators when it is mature, but before the chicks hatch or while they are chicks the tern is threatened by humans, other animals, and the tides.
The entire crown is black with a shaggy, erectable crest on the nape in the spring during courtship and the start of the breeding season.
The royal tern feeds in salt water and on very rare occasions in fresh water.
It lays one or two eggs, usually in a scrape, an area on the ground where a tern has made a small hole to lay its eggs.

It weighs about 415 g.
It feeds mostly on fish and other animals it catches in water.
It lives mostly in the open sea.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It spends most of its time in the air.
It nests in a scrape on the ground.
It lays 1 to 2 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: On a lonely island beach, where few hunters come, the royal tern makes its nest: a small hole scraped in the ground.

In spring courtship, a shaggy black crest rises on its nape, a crown fit for its name.

facts.text: Bewick's wren is a wren native to North America.

Some of its populations migrate and others stay all year.
It forages in the air, on the ground and in the trees alike.
It nests in a half cup.
It lays 3 to 8 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: A young male Bewick's wren does not sing his father's song.
He learns it from the neighboring males instead, so his tune belongs to the birds next door, not to his family.
That song is loud and tuneful, much like the songs of other wrens.
From his perch, he sings it to begin his courting.
For food, this North American wren picks insects, insect eggs and spiders from leaves and tree trunks, or finds them on the ground.

tagline.text: He sings his neighbors' song, not his father's.

facts.text: The California thrasher is a large member of family Mimidae found primarily in chaparral habitat in California in the United States and Baja California in Mexico.
The California thrasher has a distinct foraging behavior, often seeking food under dense and continuous cover.
Common raven and California scrub jay are common predators of eggs and nestlings.
The California thrasher is recognized as a "striking and exuberant songster" known for its mimicking capabilities.
The California thrasher primarily inhabits the great interior valleys of California, where it forages mainly beneath dense and continuous cover.
It primarily forages on the ground, making up approximately two-thirds of its foraging activity.
Following egg-laying, the incubation period lasts approximately 14 days.
The California thrasher is a year round resident of both slopes of the California Coast Ranges and the western slope of the Sierra Nevada.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 31 cm from its wing length.
It weighs about 84 g.
It feeds mostly on insects and other invertebrates.
It lives mostly in shrubland.
It stays in its range all year.
It forages in the air, on the ground and in the trees alike.
It nests in a cup.
It lays 3 to 4 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Down in the chaparral of California and Baja California, a large thrasher works beneath the thick brush.
About two-thirds of its foraging happens on the ground, under dense and continuous cover.
It never wanders off, staying all year on both slopes of the Coast Ranges and the Sierra Nevada's western slope.
Yet the bird hidden in the brush is a striking and exuberant songster, and a gifted mimic besides.

tagline.text: The hidden ground-seeker of the chaparral, with a borrowed song.

facts.text: The greater yellowlegs is a large shorebird in the family Scolopacidae.
They mainly eat insects and small fish, as well as crustaceans, marine worms, frogs, seeds and berries.
They nest on the ground, usually in well-hidden locations near water.
The call is harsher, louder, and clearer than that of the lesser yellowlegs.
The young leave the nest within 24 hours of hatching and then leave the vicinity of the nest within two days.
Their breeding habitat is bogs and marshes in the boreal forest region of Canada and Alaska.
They migrate to the Atlantic and Pacific coasts of the United States, the Caribbean, and south to South America.
The greater yellowlegs is similar in appearance to the smaller lesser yellowlegs.

sentences.text: Across the bogs and marshes of the northern forest rings a call harsher, louder and clearer than its smaller cousin's.
It belongs to the greater yellowlegs, a large shorebird that nests on the ground, well hidden near water.
Its chicks waste no time: they leave the nest within a day of hatching and soon wander far from it.
Then the bird flies on to the Atlantic and Pacific coasts, the Caribbean, and south to South America.

tagline.text: The loud-voiced shorebird of the northern bogs.

facts.text: The willet is a large shorebird in the family Scolopacidae.
They are territorial both on the breeding grounds and on the wintering areas but form loose breeding colonies or wintering groups.
The male normally leads the female through the territory and creates trial nest scrapes for the female to consider until she selects the site.
The willet's name is onomatopoeic and refers to its loud piercing "pill-will-willet" territorial song., which is higher pitched and repeated at a faster rate in Eastern willets than in Western birds.
The passage of the Migratory Bird Treaty Act in 1918 protected the willet from intensive exploitation by hunters for food and allowed its numbers to rebound to present levels.
When displaying the wings are held stiffly and downcurved in flight while on the ground the display gives prominence to the distinctive pattern of the underwings.
If the nest is placed among grass the female may pull grass stalks over the nest for camouflage.
The eastern willet breeds in coastal saltmarshes while the western willet breeds in freshwater prairie marshes, sloughs, potholes and other inland wetlands.

sentences.text: Pill-will-willet rings across the marsh, and so the bird named itself, for "willet" echoes that loud, piercing song.
Eastern birds, bred in coastal saltmarshes, sing it higher and faster than western birds of inland prairie marshes.
The male leads the female through his territory, scratching trial nest scrapes until she picks one.
Among grass, she may pull stalks over the nest to hide it.
A loud voice for the ground it claims, and a hidden home.

tagline.text: It sings its own name across the marsh.

facts.text: The American robin is a migratory bird of the true thrush genus and Turdidae, the wider thrush family.

sentences.text: By night the robins gather in great flocks; by day the flocks break apart, and small bands go seeking fruit and berries.

facts.text: The western kingbird is a large tyrant flycatcher found throughout western North America, as far south as Mexico.

Its throne is a sturdy cup nest, sometimes set atop a pole.

facts.text: The mourning dove is a member of the dove family, Columbidae.
